title: Apollo launches $11 billion private credit platform, backed by Abu Dhabi
description: Apollo Global Management has launched a European private credit platform with more than 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) of lending capacity, backed b
body: Apollo Global Management has launched a European private credit platform with more than 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) of lending capacity, backed by several blue-chip investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Council (ADIC).The European Credit Company will invest in performing credit across the large and mid-market sectors, including corporate and asset-backed lending, as well as lending to real-asset owners in infrastructure and real estate.The venture is led by Giacomo Petrobelli, serving as chief executive officer, and Christian Meissner, its chairman.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconApollo Global Management.Petrobelli said Apollo's ECC aims to capitalize on a "generational opportunity" to finance Europe's long-term growth agenda using global pools of capital. Apollo partners with ADIC The venture's backing from ADIC comes a week after Apollo agreed to buy a nearly 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Co., Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund.Other strategic partners in the new platform include European insurance group Athora, Japanese lender Norinchukin Bank, Standard Chartered and Aranda Principal Strategies, a U.S. credit investor, Apollo said in an announcement."We aim to build ECC into a premier pan-European credit platform, focused exclusively on the region, with deep local relationships, differentiated sourcing and flexible solutions that span all credit types," said Petrobelli."The Global Industrial Renaissance is creating tremendous financing needs around the world that are acutely felt in Europe, whether it's energy transition and transmission, defense, or digital and traditional infrastructure," added Apollo president Jim Zelter.

schema.headline: Apollo launches $11 billion private credit platform, backed by Abu Dhabi

title: Sam Altman makes surprise South Korea visit as OpenAI builds on chip partnerships
description: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAi speaks with CNBC in San Francisco on Sept. 29th, 2026. CNBCOpenAI CEO Sam Altman made an unannounced visit to South Korea ov
body: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAi speaks with CNBC in San Francisco on Sept. 29th, 2026. CNBCOpenAI CEO Sam Altman made an unannounced visit to South Korea over the weekend, meeting with Samsung executives and reportedly holding talks with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, building on existing partnerships with the country's leading chipmakers.Samsung said Saturday that Altman met with around 50 executives from its affiliates spanning electronics, finance and biotechnology in Yongin, south of Seoul.The discussions covered AI developments, potential business opportunities and the technology's impact on corporate decision-making and operations, Samsung said. Altman also met with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won over lunch Saturday, with senior executives from SK Hynix and SK Telecom in attendance, according to South Korean media reports.The two sides may have discussed cooperation on AI chips and data centers, including existing plans for high-bandwidth memory supplies and AI data center development, according to local media reports. The participants didn't provide details of the discussions.SK Hynix told CNBC it was unable to confirm the reported meeting.Altman also visited South Korea in October 2025, when he met with President Lee Jae Myung, Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee and SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and announced partnerships with Samsung and SK Group as part of OpenAI's Stargate initiative.OpenAI's Stargate initiative aims to expand AI infrastructure globally, with South Korea playing a role through partnerships focused on advanced memory chip supplies and AI data center development.Under the agreements, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix outlined plans to ramp up production of advanced memory chips, while OpenAI and its South Korean partners agreed to explore developing AI data centers in the country.OpenAI cited South Korea's ranking among global leaders in AI readiness and significant public-private funding to strengthen competitiveness as reasons for expanding its presence in the country.Altman's latest visit also follows a July meeting with Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee at OpenAI's headquarters in San Francisco, according to Samsung.Altman left South Korea on Saturday, according to local media reports.

schema.headline: Sam Altman makes surprise South Korea visit as OpenAI builds on chip partnerships

title: OpenAI deepens Abu Dhabi foothold as Sam Altman inks deals spanning energy, government and investment
description: OpenAI has signed deals across energy, investment and government sectors in the United Arab Emirates as the AI lab works to secure funding from invest
body: OpenAI has signed deals across energy, investment and government sectors in the United Arab Emirates as the AI lab works to secure funding from investors in the region as part of a $20 billion round.CEO Sam Altman met with Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, crown prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, as the artificial intelligence lab secured arrangements for a number of sectors to use its models, the Abu Dhabi Media Office said on Monday. While the Middle East has emerged as a key AI hub in recent years, with U.S. big tech companies signing deals to develop huge data centers in the region, ongoing conflict has tested that appeal. OpenAI and Anthropic have turned to Middle East investors as they've looked for ever-larger pools of capital to fund growth. MGX, an Abu Dhabi-based investment firm, has backed both labs, including co-leading Anthropic's $30 billion raise in February and OpenAI's $122 billion raise in March. OpenAI is currently seeking to raise $20 billion in a new funding round co-led by investors from the United Arab Emirates, CNBC reported on Saturday.watch now"Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone," Altman said in a statement. "We are proud to support the UAE's ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation."The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, or ADNOC, G42 signed an agreement to deploy OpenAI's frontier technology. Sovereign investor Mubadala, Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to apply advanced AI capabilities to investment analysis.The Abu Dhabi Government announced an initiative with the AI lab to translate government policies and regulations in machine-readable form. Inception42 and OpenAI also signed a five-year agreement to enable the adoption of frontier AI across government, enterprise and education.

schema.headline: OpenAI deepens Abu Dhabi foothold as Sam Altman inks deals spanning energy, government and investment

title: U.S. crude falls below $100 amid reports of U.S.-Iran diplomatic efforts
description: The Panama-flagged container shipping vessel Ten Neptune transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah in the east
body: The Panama-flagged container shipping vessel Ten Neptune transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah in the east of the UAE on Oct. 13, 2026. AFP | Getty ImagesOil prices fell sharply early on Monday amid reports that both the U.S. and Iran are seeking diplomatic options to bring an end to the Middle East conflict. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for January delivery fell 4.61% to $108.20 a barrel as of 5:49 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December declined 4.44% to $99.50 per barrel.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon Brent U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically."Trump "hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully," Rubio said, speaking to reporters over the weekend. Iranian authorities also signaled that a deal is still possible, following two days of talks mediated by Qatar, as long as demands are implemented tangibly, according to Al Jazeera. The news come following reports that both the U.S. and Iran are preparing for more military strikes after the midterm elections.Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate that the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon wtiIranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term. "Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates. "Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added. —CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

schema.headline: U.S. crude falls below $100 amid reports of U.S.-Iran diplomatic efforts

title: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy has stroke and is in the hospital, office says
description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., conducts a rally outside the U.S. Capitol to demand the Senate take action on gun safety on Thursday, May 26, 2022, in the
body: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., conducts a rally outside the U.S. Capitol to demand the Senate take action on gun safety on Thursday, May 26, 2022, in the wake of the Robb Elementary School shooting in Texas. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., appears at left.Tom Williams | CQ-Roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesSen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday.Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt."Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said.Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington."The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery."Murphy, who came to the Senate in 2013, is not up for reelection on Tuesday, but he's been crisscrossing the country campaigning for Democratic candidates, with recent stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He was due in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas.He's seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and is a prolific Democratic fundraiser.Murphy, 53, spent six years in the House before running for the Senate. He rose to national prominence as an advocate for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting, which occurred in his home state. He's been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has opposed the war in Iran and the White House's deportation policies.He's one of multiple sitting senators to suffer a stroke in recent years. Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland each had a stroke in 2022. And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., who was then running for office, suffered a stroke just days before his state's Senate Democratic primary."Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy. I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a fellow Connecticut Democrat, posted to X on Sunday.

schema.headline: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy has stroke and is in the hospital, office says

title: South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget
description: NEW YORK, UNITED STATES - SEPTEMBER 22: President of South Korea Lee Jae Myung addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, whic
body: NEW YORK, UNITED STATES - SEPTEMBER 22: President of South Korea Lee Jae Myung addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, which brings together leaders and senior representatives of UN member states in New York, United States, on September 22, 2026.  Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesSouth Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country's largest ever budget on Monday, pledging to "boldly invest in AI and future growth engines."Speaking to the National Assembly on Monday, Lee said total spending for 2027 would rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won ($610.14 billion), including 21.3 trillion won for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers — nearly double the 2026 level.A separate 4.7 trillion won will go toward developing a sovereign AI model with what Lee described as the "world's highest performance."The government also plans to invest heavily into talent, including training 2,000 specialists to "lead semiconductor design and the regional semiconductor industry," while expanding AI education for students, job seekers and existing workers.South Korea has set up university "contract departments," where students can enroll in company-linked degrees that offer pathways to jobs at firms like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix before graduation.Companies help design courses, provide financial support and recruit qualifying graduates.The record spending plan comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasts South Korea's economy will grow 3.3% in 2026, its fastest pace since the post pandemic rebound in 2021. Lee said the higher spending would result in "virtually no net increase in government debt," with newly issued bonds used to repay existing debt.The budget also increases spending on defense and social security spending for the youth. Defense expenditure is set to rise 8.2% to 73.3 trillion won."We will rapidly transform into a smart, elite, and powerful military by establishing a hybrid manned and unmanned system based on AI, robots, and drones," Lee said.South Korea's strong economic growth has been driven largely by semiconductor exports as global demand for computing power rises with the AI boom.Exports surged 93.7% from a year earlier to a record $115.3 billion in October, according to data released Sunday by the Korea Customs Service. Shipments totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surpassing the $900 billion mark for the first time. The country posted a $42.5 billion trade surplus in October, with imports rising 36% year on year to $72.8 billion.Lee said South Korea was within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports, citing strong performance in key industries including semiconductors.

schema.headline: South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget

title: Fake nuclear warnings in Ukraine as Moscow, Kyiv report separate cyberattacks on emergency apps
description: Ukraine's Air Force said Sunday its Air Alert app had been compromised after it reportedly sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv
body: Ukraine's Air Force said Sunday its Air Alert app had been compromised after it reportedly sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv and other areas.The app briefly displayed alerts for nuclear and chemical incidents, as well as warnings of street fighting, according to Reuters. The Air Force said unauthorized persons had interfered with the app's operation and that it had temporarily disabled push notifications."There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel," the Air Force said on Telegram, according to a translation.Two hours later, Russia's Ministry for Emergency Situations said its mobile app had been subject to "a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public."It was not immediately clear if the incidents were linked. CNBC has reached out to Russian and Ukrainian authorities for comment. Local ceasefire expires in Oleshky, KhersonThe alleged cyberattacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on each other's territories and infrastructure. Overnight, a local ceasefire in the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region, near the Crimean Peninsula, expired. The temporary pause in fighting allowed humanitarian aid to enter the city and the evacuation of hundreds of people who had been trapped largely without access to food, water, electricity, and medicine. It was the longest local ceasefire since the full-scale invasion began in early 2022, and both parties appeared to have honored the pause until it ended at midnight Moscow time. KHERSON, UKRAINE - OCTOBER 28: During a ceasefire, a man on a bicycle rides past residential buildings previously damaged by Russian strikes on October 28, 2026 in Kherson, Ukraine. (Photo by Ivan Antypenko/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC "UA:PBC"/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)Global Images Ukraine | Global Images Ukraine | Getty ImagesOn Monday morning, local media reported that Russian forces had struck a hospital in central Kherson, while Ukraine's General Staff of Armed Forces said Moscow had used the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city."During the ceasefire, the rotation of Russian units, the fortification of positions, the expansion of anti-drone measures along roads and increased logistics activity, including the delivery of ammunition, were recorded," the military body said early Monday.On Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said October had been the deadliest month for Russia since the invasion began in 2022.Over the past month, Russia lost 54,400 troops killed or badly wounded, "a record for any month of the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine's Defense Forces liberated 96.2 square kilometers of Ukrainian land in October – 10.4 square kilometers more than Russia captured during that time.

schema.headline: Fake nuclear warnings in Ukraine as Moscow, Kyiv report separate cyberattacks on emergency apps

title: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians
description: GERMANY - 2026/05/20: In this photo illustration, the logo of company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited is displayed on a smartphone in front of abst
body: GERMANY - 2026/05/20: In this photo illustration, the logo of company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited is displayed on a smartphone in front of abstract background on computer screen. Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesCanadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings' proposed $5.5 billion takeover of IDBI Bank is facing pushback from employees of the Indian state-owned lender and political parties in the country.On Sunday, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees called for a two-day "nationwide" strike against the sale of the bank to Fairfax. The workers' union also expressed "grave concerns" about the transparency of the sale and valuation process, according to a post on X. It is demanding that the government "cancel the privatization process" and instead focus on strengthening the bank while protecting public investment and employees' interests. Last week, Rahul Gandhi, India's leader of the opposition, extended support to the IDBI Bank employee unions opposing the takeover by Fairfax. "Public banks are not assets to be sold off, they are tools to build the nation," Gandhi said in a statement on Thursday. He added that the sale of over 60% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax goes against the commitment of previous governments to hold a 51% stake in the state-owned lender.Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, in her response said the public sector bank was handed to the government in "poor shape" and was revived through "professionalism, prudence" and recapitalization of more than 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion)."The IDBI Bank is now poised for its next phase of growth," the finance minister said. The government has previously said that the next phase of growth will be driven by a strategic investor.The Indian government on Oct.14 said the sale of over 60% of the share in IDBI will mark the largest foreign direct investment transaction in India's financial sector. Fairfax made a bid to pay 81 rupees per share for IDBI against the average fair value set at 75.99 rupees apiece.On Monday, shares of IDBI opened at around 79 rupees per share.However, Indian media outlet Businessworld on Thursday reported that government officials had suppressed the valuation of IDBI to make Fairfax's offer seem attractive. The Ministry of Finance has defended its procedure, adding that the bidding process was a "double blind" as the bidder did not know the valuation and the valuators did not see the bids.The Indian government has been divesting stakes this year as it pushes to keep the country's growth engine running amid deepening fiscal pressures. It sold shares in several companies, including Cochin Shipyard, Indian Railways Finance Corp, NHPC and Coal India. In August, it got $3.3 billion for a 6.5% stake in the country's top life insurer, Life Insurance Corporation of India.

schema.headline: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians

title: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
description: Cfoto | Future Publishing | Getty ImagesBinance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3
body: Cfoto | Future Publishing | Getty ImagesBinance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform.The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X. The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28.Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial. The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets."Circle activated its incident response procedures and coordinated with law enforcement to freeze more than $1.1 billion in USDC associated with the incident," a spokesperson for the stablecoin issuer told CNBC in an email. The company said the investigation is ongoing.The updated figure follows a Friday post from Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire, who said at the time that more than $800 million in USDC linked to the incident had been frozen.Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added.The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor. The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users.Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

schema.headline: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack

title: The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know
description: Voters fill out their ballots at an early voting polling place at Lynnhurst Recreation Center on Oct. 28, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Stephen Matur
body: Voters fill out their ballots at an early voting polling place at Lynnhurst Recreation Center on Oct. 28, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Stephen Maturen | Getty ImagesThe outcome of Tuesday's election is expected to have broad implications across the market, including municipal bonds. The spotlight has been on the battle for congressional control and whether Democrats will wrest the House of Representatives, the Senate or both from Republicans. But for the muni market, what happens at the state level could have bigger repercussions — at least in the near term. There is an array of initiatives on ballots around the nation that could change tax laws and add to bond supply. Taxes matter to muni investors since the income received is free of federal tax, as well as state tax if the holder lives in the state where the bond is issued.Red vs. blue taxes Depending on the location, ballot measures are up for approval that would either provide tax breaks, or raise taxes on the wealthy. "It's a complete bifurcation between red and blue states," said Dan Close, head of municipals at Nuveen. "Blue states are trying to put in place graduated income tax structures, trying to capture more revenue from high-income earners. Red states are promoting affordability by trying to cut property taxes."Red states are those that predominantly vote Republican, while blue states swing toward Democrats. For instance, California has a proposition known as the "billionaire tax," which would impose a one-time levy equal to 5% of the wealth of certain taxpayers with at least $1 billion in assets. The state also has a measure on the ballot that would make a temporary tax hike permanent on individuals earning over $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031. "The impact to the muni bond market will be to make the exemption more valuable," Close said of the possible passage of tax increases. Investors will likely seek shelter in the muni market, which would send bond prices higher, he noted.It is a different story in Florida, where voters are set to decide whether to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Qualified homeowners currently have a $25,000 property tax exemption, as well as another for $25,000 that doesn't apply to school property taxes. The new proposal raises the latter exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 by 2028. New residents have a five-year waiting period before receiving the benefit.  If passed, some local governments will have to find other revenue sources or increase the overall tax rate to replace what they've lost, said Tom Kozlik, head of public policy and municipal strategy at HilltopSecurities."It's not necessarily going to result in downgrades for sure, but there would have to be some balancing with regard to overall revenues," he said.Not all municipalities will be hurt equally, which means credit research is important, said Close."Like everything in municipal finance, it is really on a case-by-case basis that you could have some credit deterioration from [a] rollback of property taxes," he said. Increased supplyOther voters on Tuesday will be asked to approve more state or local government debt. That could weigh on a market that has already seen heightened supply. Some $473.8 billion has already been issued year to date, through September, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. That's a 7.8% increase over the same period a year ago. In 2025, total muni issuance reached $587.3 billion, 14.3% higher than 2024, Sifma said. Cooper Howard, director of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, believes supply is the biggest issue coming out of the election. "That amount of issuance has been one of the reasons why you have to see that strong amount of demand continue to keep pace with it for total returns to keep up," Howard said. Fortunately, new supply doesn't necessarily come quickly into the market. "There's a window over a couple years that they can issue," he noted. The ultimate makeup of the next Congress could also have consequences for muni investors as lawmakers sort out their priorities. Most notable is what lawmakers will do to tackle the country's affordability problem, Kozlik at Hilltop said. "There could be some tax policy initiatives and even affordability-related initiatives that manifest themselves in the first quarter of next year," he said. "That could impact housing. It could impact higher education. It could impact public power financing."Opportunities now Investors considering moves before the election may want to look at those states with tax increases on the ballot, said Close at Nuveen.For instance, Nuveen recently began offering a separately managed account dedicated to Washington after getting an enormous number of inquiries from financial advisors. The state recently enacted a 9.9% tax on individuals with taxable annual income above $1 million, set to go into effect in 2028. But the issue is now being put to voters, who can decide whether to repeal the new law.  "At the margin, if you do think that some of these measures are going to pass, knowing that bonds usually move up with an increase in taxes, there might be some opportunities to buy ahead of the election for blue states," Close said.Howard believes munis are attractive right now, particularly for those who are in a tax bracket of 24% or above. Fundamentals are good and the bonds largely have good credit quality, he said. "About 70% of the broad muni index is either triple-A or double-A rated."Kozlik is also bullish, calling yields "really attractive." He suggests investors concentrate on AA-rated or higher bonds. "The muni space is part of the portfolio that most investors want," he said. "It helps them sleep well at night."

schema.headline: The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know

title: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries
description: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without interventi
body: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without intervention before then, the Social Security retirement trust fund, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which helps pay benefits to eligible workers and qualifying family members, will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, the program's trustees said in a June report.At that time, the trustees project retirement benefits will be cut by 22%.The Congressional Budget Office has a more dire forecast, anticipating the retirement trust fund may run out sooner, in mid-2032, and that retirees may see larger benefit cuts, at 26%, upon insolvency. Beneficiaries may see an average $500 cut to their monthly benefits across the U.S. based on a 24% benefit cut, according to a June report from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. In 29 states, retirees would see even bigger average reductions, according to the nonpartisan organization focused on educating the public on fiscal policy issues. Senators elected this November will be in office in 2032, when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits. Their ability to right the ship is crucial for retirees and the economy. But it's not a sure thing given the political climate inside the beltway."The attention on 2032 is appropriate in the sense that that is when beneficiaries and future beneficiaries will see and feel the consequences of inaction," said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a public policy think tank focused on promoting bipartisan cooperation."Nothing gets Congress to move like that type of deadline," he said.Of course, brinksmanship and political deadlock may stymie efforts. Congress could opt to kick the can down the road, rather than enact changes to shore up Social Security — which may require tax increases, benefit cuts or a combination of both.If lawmakers decide to combine Social Security's retirement and disability trust funds, the depletion date may move to the third quarter of 2034, when benefits may be cut by 17%, according to Social Security's trustees.Akabas said any delay by lawmakers would have consequences: Social Security's shortfall would continue to increase. There could also be consequences for the economy, he said.In 2023, Social Security benefits generated $2.6 trillion in total economic output and supported more than 12 million jobs, according to 2025 research by the National Institute on Retirement Security, a Washington, D.C., based non-profit, non-partisan organization.A 19% benefit cut could reduce gross domestic product by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to the NIRS research.Moreover, failing to muster Social Security reform would prompt bond market strain, according to research published in June by George Mason University's Mercatus Center. Social Security is tied to the bond market because its trust funds are invested in special issue U.S. Treasury bonds. If Social Security reform is delayed, that may put upward pressure on Treasury yields, with investors wanting higher returns for long-term bonds. Delayed reform may either prompt higher interest rates and borrowing costs or inflationary adjustments that hurt the value of government liabilities, according to the Mercatus Center research. Those changes may affect household budgets through higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer credit, as well as student loans, according to the research. If interest rates and prices rise, that will interfere with economic growth, Akabas said."Those effects are also ones that the American people feel, in addition to adjustments to their benefits," Akabas said.Heading to the midterms, some Democratic congressional candidates have said they would raise or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap so high earners pay more into the program. In 2026, the 6.2% tax paid by both workers and their employers applies to earnings up to $184,500.Yet it remains to be seen whether Washington leaders will have the political will to address the problem soon. Tax increases, in particular, may not be viewed as politically popular heading into the 2028 presidential election.As such, payroll taxes are "extraordinarily unlikely" to rise in the next couple of years, said Jessica Riedl, a fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, which provides independent analyses of tax issues. If those tax hikes happen, it would likely be closer to 2032, she said."In Washington, they love to wait until the last minute," Riedl said. "There's no interest on either side for these sorts of tax increases in the short term. In the long term, I think everything is on the table."The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, founded by President Franklin Delano Roosevelt's son, former Congressman James Roosevelt, has scored incumbent lawmakers on whether their votes have protected those programs.The advocacy organization has also endorsed candidates that support raising payroll taxes and protecting Social Security benefits from cuts. With those endorsements, NCPSSM gives candidates a set of boxing gloves as a symbol of the fights they'll face in Congress, according to Dan Adcock, NCPSSM's director of government relations and policy.The organization is also working to educate voters that the senators elected this year will be among those to deal with Social Security, he said."We've been trying to impress upon voters why this is an issue that should be top tier," Adcock said. "They need to be asking candidates about what their plans for the program would be."

schema.headline: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries

title: Ryanair CEO warns fares could rise by up to 20% in 2027 as fuel bill jumps by $2.2 billion
description: watch nowRyanair CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC Monday that European airfares are set to rise "significantly," growing by as much as 20% next year as f
body: watch nowRyanair CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC Monday that European airfares are set to rise "significantly," growing by as much as 20% next year as fuel hedges expire.The budget air carrier's profit fell 15% to 2.15 billion euros ($2.3 billion) in the first fiscal half of the year, as the price of its 20% unhedged jet fuel doubled. "So we're facing 2027 where we have much higher oil prices... I think they're going to get passed on in significantly higher airfares," O'Leary told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick on Monday. "The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months... but those hedges are rolling off. There's still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we're all facing next year. I believe you're going to see airfares rise next year across Europe by 10%, maybe even 20%," O'Leary added. Ryanair said it doesn't expect an increase in short-haul airfares to fully offset an estimated 2-billion-euro increase in fuel charges next year. It is therefore launching a cost review, which will include lowering crew rations, a potential temporary pay freeze and the use of AI to drive further efficiencies.Ryanair's Irish-listed shares initially edged higher in early Monday trading before paring gains to trade below the flatline. The stock has fallen over 22% this year.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconRyanair stock since the beginning of the year. The airline said in September it would cut its full-year traffic target from 216 million passengers to 214 million passengers in a bid to reduce its exposure to unhedged fuel during the winter. It's now expecting winter traffic between November and March to remain broadly flat year-on-year."I think you're seeing even this winter, all of the airlines across Europe, even Ryanair, for the first time in many years, we cut our winter capacity," O'Leary said. We'll only be flat this winter over the prior year, because it makes no sense for us to be growing capacity if we're buying unhedged oil at $170 a barrel."Ryanair hedged 80% of its jet fuel at $67 per barrel for the year, which it said gave it an advantage over its competitors as its earnings remained insulated from volatile oil prices. The carrier added that it has hedged at least 25% of its 2028 jet fuel prices at $95 per barrel. Earnings remain 'hostage' to oil pricesThe share price reaction on Monday says more about investors' expectations than the numbers alone, according to Adam Vetesse, market analyst at eToro."Investors appear to have already priced in the hit from unhedged fuel and softer summer fares, leaving room for relief that the quarter landed exactly where consensus had predicted," Vetesse said. "Near-term earnings remain hostage to oil prices and close-in bookings, but the market's early bounce suggests investors are willing to give Ryanair the benefit of the doubt that its cost advantage will matter more than the fuel spike once the dust settles," he added. Ryanair also noted in Monday's announcement that it held 2.6 billion euros in cash as of 30 September, even after repaying 1.3 billion euros in debt. "You know we've paid off all of our debt this year, so we have effectively zero debt. We have 650 aircraft on the balance sheet. We're significantly cash positive," O'Leary told CNBC, adding that the challenge facing all airlines is the volatility in oil prices, lack of hedging, and higher financing costs. "So you see, some of our competitors are doing sale and leasebacks to generate cash. They're just mortgaging their futures; they're Ponzi schemes."

title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution
description: SpaceX is building a massive gas turbine power plant in Southaven, Mississippi to power its data centers in the area.SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, l
body: SpaceX is building a massive gas turbine power plant in Southaven, Mississippi to power its data centers in the area.SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday. The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis. The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years.The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026. The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby." (SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.)The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit. Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional.The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed."The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.watch now

title: Gen Z is ditching bars for run clubs — and finding more than friends along the way
description: watch nowQUEENS, NEW YORK — Diplo, the globally famous disc jockey, has become accustomed to performing in front of audiences wearing glitzy outfits a
body: watch nowQUEENS, NEW YORK — Diplo, the globally famous disc jockey, has become accustomed to performing in front of audiences wearing glitzy outfits and clutching alcoholic beverages in the dark. Some of his recent shows have looked very different. Swap the cocktails for electrolytes, the swanky clothes for athleisure and the nightclubs for sunny public parks. The Grammy Award-winner's team hosts five-kilometer races across the globe branded as "Diplo's Run Club." After runners cross the finish line, they enter a post-race festival that includes cold plunges, peptide product samples and a Diplo-led dance party. About 12,000 participants paid entry fees starting at around $70 — and up to about $250 for a VIP experience — for last week's race in the New York City borough of Queens.Younger American adults are spending less at bars and staying home more than their older counterparts. That's left them with fewer close friends and, during the pandemic, led to what's being called a "loneliness epidemic" that has persisted in the years since. But one type of experience appears to be getting them out of the house and socializing: sporting leagues and organized races."There's a big generational shift right now, with young people realizing that they want to spend their time working on themselves and their bodies," Diplo told CNBC ahead of the New York City event. About seven out of every 10 adults under 30 say they anticipate participating in a recreational sports league over the next six months, according to a survey from polling firm CivicScience earlier this year. Across all age groups, 37% of respondents planned on joining a league, up five percentage points from 2025. Volo Sports, an operator of recreational leagues, is on track to have 950,000 total player registrations for sports like volleyball, kickball and soccer this year. That would be an increase of around 34% from the 710,000 registrations last year and almost 500% from the 160,000 seen in 2019.Volo has attracted private-equity investors and gone on a buying spree to snap up smaller competitors in recent years. But Giovanni Marcantoni, Volo's founder and CEO, told CNBC that about three-fourths of its growth has come from organic expansion, rather than through acquisitions, as more Americans look for ways to build community."I think 'Volo,' I think 'friends,'" said Marcantoni, who met his wife through a recreational bocce league. "Both those things put a smile on your face, and that's what our goal is as a brand." Volo participants compete in a soccer league.Photo: Kevin Heitczman at Volo SportsDemand from young consumersThe communal fitness fervor among young adults extends to categories like cardiovascular exercise that have historically been viewed as individual affairs, but younger runners have found a way to make it more social by joining clubs and signing up for organized races. On social media, some users joke that partaking in distance running or other endurance-based competitions is now a "quarter-life crisis."The share of finishers of the New York City Marathon in their 20s neared 24% in 2025, up from about 15% in 2019. New York Road Runners, the nonprofit behind the marathon, told CNBC that 27% of registered runners for the 2026 race, which takes place this weekend, are twenty-somethings. Participation by runners in their 20s in the Chicago Marathon and the Boston Marathon has also been on the rise in recent years, according to the organizers of those races.And Ironman said a quarter of total participants in its half and full-distance triathlons are under 30 years old, an increase from 13% a decade ago. This age group is Ironman's fastest-growing market in North America.Gen Z was 39% more likely than Gen X to say they used fitness to meet people who share their interests, according to a 2025 survey from fitness tracking platform Strava. A year prior, a Strava survey found that nearly one out of every five Gen Z respondents said they went on a date with someone they met through exercise.Hyrox, which runs fitness competitions that mix running with strength work, is leaning into its role as a potential matchmaker. It has teamed up with a dating app called Surf Dating to connect users of the platform for blind dates in its doubles competition. Participants meet for the first time just before they undergo a series of one-kilometer runs interspersed with workout stations.Surf Dating hosts a collaboration with Hyrox during a competition.Courtesy: Surf DatingSurf also hands out special wristbands to singles at Hyrox events to help them advertise their relationship status, and hosts post-race parties for them to mingle."Matching with someone based off a shared interest or passion is a better way to meet your person than hot-or-not swiping," said Rob Long, Surf's co-founder and CEO.Demand from young consumers has helped power postpandemic expansions for some traditional gyms like Life Time and workout studios such as Solidcore. But not all businesses are feeling the same tailwinds. SoulCycle has shuttered studios in recent years, and Xponential Fitness divested from underperforming brands such as CycleBar, Rumble and Row House over the last few years.'Barstools to barbells'Spending by Gen Z and millennials on fitness-related categories rose at a sharper rate year over year in early 2026 than bars, according to a report from Bank of America released earlier this year. Gen X and older generations did the opposite, with bar spending climbing at a faster clip in the period tracked by the bank.Said another way: Younger cohorts are shifting "from barstools to barbells," according to Joe Wadford, an economist at Bank of America. It's part of a longer-term trend of Americans drinking less and less, sending the share of people who say they consume alcohol to record lows.Still, organizers of these athletic events aren't writing off booze entirely. Volo partners with bars to offer deals for players looking to fraternize before or after their matches. Diplo's Run Club had several bars in the post-race festival selling cocktails and beer."I definitely don't think there's a death to drinking," said Autumn Rossi, a 30-year-old sales analyst who came to Diplo's race from New Jersey. "I think people are just doing it in a different way, which is important."Brody Short identifies as one of those young people shifting her time and spending toward community-based fitness. After struggling to convince people in her social circle to forgo late nights at bars for early weekend mornings spent running and at hot yoga classes, the 26-year-old founded a run club called Energy in Liberty Lake, Washington.Beyond meeting each week for runs, Short's club organizes fundraisers for local nonprofits and cheering squads when members are partaking in organized races. Short is a bridesmaid and maid of honor in upcoming weddings of friends she met through the club. "It's deeper than the running," Short said. "I didn't start it just so every Tuesday I could run three miles with somebody I didn't know. I did it because I wanted to meet friends. I wanted to find real people that I could integrate into my life."Participants in an Outlast event hold an Energy Run Club flag.Source: Brody ShortWhen talking with older generations, Short said she typically fields questions about whether she's dating someone or hopes to have children soon. After she responds no, Short said follow-up questions focus on how she's filling her time instead."We're not raising kids," Short said. "What are we doing? Well, I guess we're running marathons and doing Hyrox."And they're dancing — at least at the run clubs that Diplo is hosting. The DJ, born Wes Pentz, says the run clubs he hosts are a blast, but he also has a more selfish motivation: As the 47-year-old ages, he can opt to work fewer late nights. "I don't want to spend the rest of my career playing into the night until 4 in the morning," Diplo said. "I want to build this brand where I can have these parties in the daytime." Participants run through the Pilsen neighborhood during the 2025 Chicago Marathon in Chicago, Illinois, on October 12, 2025. Octavio Jones | Afp | Getty Images

schema.headline: Gen Z is ditching bars for run clubs — and finding more than friends along the way

title: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier
description: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about a
body: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesAnthropic picked a tough week to unveil its IPO prospectus. Within days of its release, several of the company's key partners, including Microsoft, Google and Amazon, reported quarterly results that added fuel to existing market jitters around the artificial intelligence buildout. "Everybody's still full steam ahead on AI, but all the things around it took an interesting turn this week," Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, told CNBC in an interview on Friday. The hyperscalers' results have "raised eyebrows" and created a new headwind in the market, which is "more doubt on capital structure," he said. No matter the current state of the market, Anthropic was going to have to address a skeptical investor base as it pursues a potentially record-setting initial public offering in the coming weeks. In its prospectus on Monday, the AI company disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors. Investors are still waiting to see Anthropic's third-quarter financials. Heading into this week, fears were mounting about the financial health of neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, which are facing rising borrowing costs and a dearth of lenders as they pursue aggressive AI buildouts. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. Now investors are growing increasingly worried about the whole AI trade.  "It's a great technology, seems to do things that we never would have imagined, but how does that then translate into a viable business?" David Hsu, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, said in an interview.The Nasdaq Composite notched its first three-week losing streak since March after plunging 2.9% on Friday. Nvidia, whose graphics processing units have powered the AI boom, traded lower, along with the whole semiconductor sector, after Intel issued a weak forecast, sending its stock to its steepest drop since the 1970s. Microsoft, Google and Amazon all had notes of concern this week in their reports. The companies have been on a spending blitz in recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts that came in below analysts' estimates. Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance for up to $205 billion and Amazon reiterated its roughly $220 billion forecast."It's been an ugly reporting season for tech thus far," Jonathan Krinsky, managing director at BTIG, wrote in a Thursday note. He described the fallout as "The Techsas Chainsaw Massacre," adding that there's too much weakness in the sector for the market to ignore. Cash is becoming an issue. Amazon reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing 12-month period. Google reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, one reason the stock tanked almost 13% on Thursday, its worst day ever. Microsoft maintained positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion, but it's down significantly for a second straight quarter. The company announced plans on Thursday to raise $25 billion in bonds, as it seeks additional sources of funding to help finance its infrastructure expansion. "Suddenly, they're like, 'We can't keep funding this on free cash flow,'" Newman said. "The worry is that basically now there's no company that's able to do this using their own business capabilities to create cash flow. It's becoming increasingly alarming."Cloud growth remains strongAnthropic's hyperscaler partners are also among its biggest investors. The companies all need each other to keep the flywheel turning, a topic that's sure to be a major point of discussion in Anthropic's upcoming roadshow. Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. A big tail wind for Anthropic remains AI demand. Microsoft, Google and Amazon all reported cloud growth that topped analysts' estimates, with revenue in Google's business more than doubling from a year earlier. And Oracle, one of the biggest spenders on AI data centers, said at its investor day on Wednesday that it will limit additional fundraising in the coming years to $20 billion, and will turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year. Analysts at Citizens wrote in a Thursday report that the announcement "put the biggest investor fear to rest — that funding its enormous AI infrastructure buildout would require an open-ended increase in debt and equity issuance."watch nowAttention will now turn back from hyperscaler earnings to Anthropic, as investors assess how much risk they're willing to assume and at what price. The IPO market has largely been frozen since SpaceX's record offering in June. Biometric ring maker Oura, Australian AI data center operator Firmus and SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm subsidiary have all recently postponed or abandoned plans to IPO. Nscale, a neocloud that filed to go public in September, hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks, nor has SoftBank's SB Energy. With Anthropic, Newman said the FOMO — fear of missing out — on a potentially "generational" company is real, and that the prospectus was "very impressive," showing 1,300% annual sales growth, 900% net revenue retention and an implied gross margin of 85%.  "Anthropic is the IPO market at this point," Newman said. "I think companies would have to be extremely cautious, if not just foolish, to actually want to come out in this period."— CNBC's Jordan Novet, Annie Palmer and Samantha Subin contributed to this report.WATCH: Anthropic’s heavy AI spending could hold the key to its profitability: Ark Investwatch now
